Learning Objectives
Understand the mechanics of a normal glenohumeral joint compared with a rotator cuff–
deficient joint and glenohumeral joint managed via reverse shoulder arthroplasty.
Understand how reverse shoulder arthroplasty component placement and design are used to
improve shoulder kinematics.
Understand complications associated with the biomechanics of reverse shoulder arthroplasty
prosthesis design.

Normal Shoulder Mechanics
The glenohumeral joint lacks osseous stability from bony congruency and, therefore, relies on
soft-tissue restraint for stability.
The rotator cuff is primarily responsible for compressive forces of the humeral head on the
glenoid.
In rotator cuff–deficient shoulders, the imbalance of the continued pull of the deltoid
compared with the lack of compressive forces from the rotator cuff musculature leads to
proximal migration of the humerus with wear of the glenoid, acromion, humeral head.

Normal Shoulder Mechanics
A normal glenohumeral joint, which lacks inherent osseous stability provided by
congruent bony morphology, allows for motions that are not present in many other
joints.1 These motions have been described as spinning (rotation), sliding (translation),
and rolling (rotation and translation).2 Therefore, stability of the glenohumeral joint is
provided by soft-tissue restraints and compressive forces of the humeral head on the
glenoid. The rotator cuff muscles function primarily to balance this compressive load and
maintain stability of the glenohumeral joint. This is most important during shoulder
motion to maintain stability and resist proximal translational forces of the deltoid during
abduction and elevation.3
In patients with a rotator cuff–deficient shoulder, the compressive forces of the humeral
head against the glenoid become imbalanced. With additional loss of rotator cuff
integrity because of tearing and fatty degeneration, the rotator cuff muscles are unable
to adequately counter the forces from the muscles around the shoulder that are
primarily responsible for motion, such as the deltoid. This ultimately leads to proximal
migration of the humeral head and may result in eccentric wear of the glenoid,
acromion, and proximal humerus. This constellation of findings has been termed rotator
cuff tear arthropathy.4

Reverse shoulder arthroplasty was first designed in the 1970s for the management of rotator
cuff tear arthropathy.
Early designs placed the center of rotation lateral to the glenoid fossa, leading to excessive
torque on the glenoid bone interface and resulting in fixation failure and glenoid component
loosening.
Initially developed as a salvage procedure, reverse shoulder arthroplasty currently is a
common treatment option for the management of rotator cuff tear arthropathy, glenohumeral
joint arthritis with glenoid bone deficiency, massive rotator cuff tears, proximal humerus
fractures, malunion and nonunion of the proximal humerus, and other complex conditions of
the shoulder.

History of Reverse Shoulder Arthroplasty Designs
Reverse shoulder arthroplasty designs, which were first introduced in the 1970s, were
primarily intended to manage pain and improve function in patients with rotator cuff
tear arthropathy. Reverse shoulder arthroplasty was initially developed as a salvage
procedure; however, the use of the prosthesis has broadened in the past few decades.
Reverse shoulder arthroplasty currently is commonly used to manage not only rotator
cuff tear arthropathy but also glenohumeral joint osteoarthritis. Reverse shoulder
arthroplasty also is used to manage posterior glenoid deficiency, massive rotator cuff
tears, proximal humerus fractures, malunion and nonunion, and other complex
conditions of the shoulder.5 The prosthesis was originally designed to resist superior
migration of the humeral head by creating a fixed fulcrum for the joint. The congruency
of the components is intended to restrict translation or rolling while preserving spinning
(rotational) motions.
Early designs placed the center of rotation lateral to the glenoid fossa, which is similar to
that of normal glenohumeral joint anatomy. This led to excessive torque and shear
stress on the interface between the glenoid bone and glenosphere fixation.6 These early
designs primarily focused on resisting the pathologic forces; however, they did not
adequately account for the force placed on the components, leading to early component
fixation failure.

Grammont and Baulot developed their reverse shoulder prosthesis in 1985 (Figure 1).
The four key principals of Grammont’s original design were that (1) the center of rotation
must be fixed, distalized, and medialized to the level of the glenoid surface; (2) the
prosthesis must be inherently stable; (3) the lever arm of the deltoid must be effective
from the start of movement; and (4) the glenosphere must be large and the humeral
head cup must be small to create a semiconstrained articulation.6-8 The prosthetic
design was later modified to become the Delta III reverse shoulder prosthesis (DePuy),
which was released in 19919 (Figure 2). This design medialized the humeral center of
rotation to the level of the glenoid face to reduce stress on the glenoid-bone interface.
Locking screw fixation was added later to improve glenoid baseplate fixation. This model
improved the fixation of the glenosphere, decreasing failure from baseplate loosening,
which was observed with earlier designs. A 42-mm hemispheric glenosphere with the
center of rotation at the glenoid face in combination with a 155° valgus neck-shaft angle
of the proximal humerus at resulted in a medial and inferior center of rotation for the
joint. Although this design showed promising clinical results, scapular notching because
of bony impingement between the medial humerus and the inferior scapula and
limitations in external rotation remained problematic.3 Designs have evolved to manage
postoperative complications, such as component loosening, scapular notching,
component wear, and bony impingement. The goals of these changes are to improve
clinical and functional outcomes, such as increasing range of motion and strength with
forward elevation and rotation.10,11

Biomechanics of Reverse Shoulder Arthroplasty
Guiding Principles
Reverse shoulder arthroplasty is a nonanatomic implant reconstruction procedure that
intentionally alters the kinematics of the glenohumeral joint to reduce pain and improve
function.

6/33

A congruent prosthetic design that limits translational motion and allows for rotational motion
is used to account for the effects of the loss of the rotator cuff.
The joint center of rotation is moved medial, and in some designs, inferior to alter the
kinematics of the glenohumeral joint.

Guiding Principles
The reverse shoulder arthroplasty implant design was initially created to prevent wear
on the acromion, coracoid, superior glenoid, and humeral head that was caused by
proximal migration of the humerus. The prosthesis was intended to resist the proximal
pull of the deltoid in patients in whom the rotator cuff was deficient.2
Function of the joint is restored via a construct that is conforming in its componentry
design to limit joint motion to rotation. The congruency of the prosthesis restricts sliding
or rolling motions. Muscles allow for joint motion by exerting force and tension. This can
be created via contraction, or shortening in the muscle, or via tension caused by
stretching of the muscle fibers past the resting length.2 Muscle straight-line force is
converted into torque and rotational force around the center of rotation. The amount of
torque is proportional to the perpendicular distance between the center of rotation and
the line of muscle action, referred to as the moment arm.2 An increase in the length of
the moment arm would therefore decrease the required force by the muscle to exert the
same amount of rotational torque (Figure 3).
Although increasing the moment arm may result in increased torque, greater excursion
of the muscle also is required to generate motion. Other factors of the muscle also must
be considered in assessing its ability to create force. These include the cross-sectional
area, the architecture of the muscle, and the length-tension relationship.2

Glenoid Center of Rotation
The humeral center of rotation is moved medial toward the glenoid surface.
In addition to decreasing implant stress at the interface of the glenoid and baseplate,
medialization allows for functional improvement of the deltoid.
Grammont design also moves the center of rotation inferior, resulting in additional deltoid
tensioning.

Glenoid Center of Rotation
Perhaps the most notable design principle of reverse shoulder arthroplasty is
medialization of the center of rotation of the glenohumeral joint toward the glenoid
surface. The optimal amount of medialization continues to be a topic of debate.
Medialization of the center of rotation allows for functional use of the deltoid by
increasing the deltoid lever arm and allowing for enhanced muscle fiber recruitment3,7
(Figure 4). In addition, this also results in decreased implant stress at the interface
between the glenoid bone and the component baseplate.

Although fixation was improved with medialization, other challenges with this design
were noted. These include decreased range of motion from bony impingement, scapular
notching from impingement of the medial humerus on the inferior scapula, and
decreased active motion and external rotation strength caused by loss of tension on the
rotator cuff muscles. Another complication of medialization is loss of the normal deltoid
contour of the shoulder, which affects cosmetic appearance and symmetry (Figure 5).

The center of rotation is determined by the difference between the glenosphere
thickness and the glenosphere articular radius. The Grammont reverse shoulder
prosthesis uses a glenosphere that is equivalent in its radius and thickness. Therefore,
the center of rotation is 0 mm and is placed at the surface of the glenosphere fixation.
Lateralization of the glenosphere is achieved by increasing the thickness of the
glenosphere relative to its articular radius2 (Figure 6).

The glenoid center of rotation can be lateralized via glenosphere design, baseplate
design including augmentation, and the use of bone graft between the baseplate and
the glenoid. This technique has been described as bony increased-offset reverse
shoulder arthroplasty and was proposed as a method of lateralizing the implant while
limiting the distance of the center of rotation from the bone-implant interface14 (Figures
9 and 10). Lateral designs have demonstrated improvement in external rotation
function, component stability, and decreased scapular notching; however, increased
torque and shear stress on the glenoid baseplate-bone interface also are observed with
this construct.

Lateralized designs also can be used to restore optimal medialization of the center of
rotation. In patients who have severe glenoid wear with medialization because of bony
erosion, placement of a medialized center of rotation prosthesis may result in excessive
medialization of the center of rotation. Lateralization, whether via glenosphere design,
baseplate design, or bone graft, may be used in these patients to restore the center of
rotation to the native glenoid surface location that was present before medial bony
erosion.
Humeral Lengthening
Distalization of the humerus provides increased deltoid tensioning. This increases compressive
forces between the socket and the glenosphere to improve the stability of the prosthesis.
Humeral lengthening increases the deltoid lever arm and deltoid muscle tensioning to improve
function.

Humeral Lengthening
In addition to medially shifting the center of rotation of the joint, the Grammont design
also inferiorly shifts the center of rotation. The original Grammont prosthesis used a
155° valgus neck-shaft angle to distalize the humerus. This functions to elongate and
tension the deltoid and increase the moment arm of the anterior, middle, and posterior
heads of the muscle to improve function2,10 (Figure 11).

Figure 11 Diagram shows a medialized humerus (left) with a neck shaft angle of 155°
and inset liner and a lateralized humerus (right) achieved with the use of a neck shaft

By moving the humerus more distal, compressive forces between the socket and the
glenosphere are increased, theoretically resulting in improved stability of the prosthesis.
However, concern exists that elongating the deltoid may lead to loss of deltoid contour
and decreased wrapping of the deltoid around the tuberosities, resulting in reduced
stability of the joint.2
Other challenges of deltoid lengthening include complications such as acromial stress
fractures, brachial plexopathy or neurapraxia caused by stretch injuries, and cosmetic
concerns.15

Lengthening of the humerus also alters the pull of the anterior and posterior rotator cuff
compared with the center of rotation. In a normal shoulder, the subscapularis anteriorly
and infraspinatus posteriorly span the center of rotation. As the humerus is distalized,
these tendons become positioned inferior to the center of rotation, leading them to
function primarily as adductors throughout the entire arc of motion.16
Lateralization with Humeral Components
Humeral lateralization may improve tuberosity positioning, improve intact rotator cuff tension,
and increase impingement-free range of motion.

Lateralization with Humeral Components
Restoring the lateral position of the humeral tuberosities is important for tensioning of
the remaining intact portion of the rotator cuff muscles. This helps restore rotational
function and stability of the prosthesis.2 The Grammont design decreases anterior and
posterior rotator cuff muscle tension by as much as 45%.17 Lateralization of the
humerus also decreases bony impingement, allowing for greater range of motion.
Humeral lateralization increases the deltoid moment arm to generate abduction,
improve rotational movement of the anterior and posterior rotator cuff, and improve the
movement arm of the posterior deltoid.18,19
The humerus can be lateralized without altering the joint center of rotation via humeral
component design. This can achieve similar goals as glenoid lateralization while avoiding
increased torque and stress at the glenoid baseplate-bone interface. Lateralized humeral
components with medial glenosphere components are associated with lower rates of
acromial and scapular spine fracture compared with lateralized glenoids20 (Figure 12).
Challenges with humeral lateralization include difficulty with subscapularis tendon repair
and healing because of lengthening and tension on the repair.

Prosthesis Design
Glenoid Baseplate Fixation
Glenoid fixation involves compression of the baseplate to the glenoid face with
osteointegration of the components.
Designs include central peg versus central compression screw with various peripheral screw
configurations with locking and nonlocking capabilities.

Glenoid Baseplate Fixation
Glenoid baseplate fixation involves compression at the baseplate of the glenoid surface
with osteointegration of the components. Cement fixation of the baseplate in reverse

shoulder arthroplasty is not popular because of high failure rates. This is in contrast to
the fixation of anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty glenoid components, which are
commonly cemented. Various osteointegration baseplate designs are available that
include central peg versus central compression screw with peripheral screw
configurations, including nonlocking and locking capabilities.21 Central screw fixation
provides increased compressive force of the baseplate to the glenoid surface compared
with central post design with the use of peripheral screws. An increase in load to failure
is associated with the central screw compared with central post design.22 Multiple
biomechanical studies continue to be conducted to optimize the configuration of
baseplate implantation and screw design.23-25 Variable-angle locking screws are
incorporated into many designs to accommodate screw trajectory toward three major
columns in the scapula. These include the base of the coracoid, the scapular spine, and
the lateral scapular pillar.26 The initial fixation of the baseplate screws has been shown
to be the most important factor for long-term fixation and osteointegration.6
Augmented baseplates have been designed for management of glenoid deformity and
bony defects. Bone graft also can be placed behind the baseplate for deformity
management.27 For severe glenoid deformity, patient-specific glenoid implants are
commercially available.28
Glenosphere Design and Placement
Grammont design glenospheres place the center rotation at the glenosphere-bone interface.
Lateralized glenospheres have increased thickness compared with radius, which allows the
center of rotation to be lateral to the glenoid face.
The intention of lateralization is to improve abduction and adduction without glenohumeral
impingement, improve stability, and improve lengthening and tensioning of the remaining
intact posterior rotator cuff musculature.

Glenosphere Design and Placement

Glenosphere designs can be grouped into two major categories. The first group contains
glenospheres that place the center of rotation at the glenosphere-bone interface. They
are based on the original Grammont design, in which the glenosphere thickness is equal
to the articular radius. The second group are glenospheres that lateralize the center of
rotation away from the glenosphere-bone interface, in which the glenoid thickness is
greater than the articular radius. This allows for placement of the center of rotation
closer to the anatomic center of rotation.3,29,30
Although placement of the glenoid component s along the inferior glenoid rim to reduce
bony impingement of the component on the scapular neck and avoid scapular notching
is well accepted, glenosphere positioning continues to be an area of interest.5,29,31 A
series of early failures with lateralized glenospheres found high failure rates with
superiorly tilted baseplates, which was common in patients with superior eccentric bone
wear.32 A study comparing neutral inclination to 15° of superior tilt with 15° degrees of
inferior tilt reported that baseplates and glenospheres placed with inferior tilt
demonstrated improvement of compressive forces with less micromotion.33 This often is
achieved via eccentric reaming of the inferior glenoid. With severe superior glenoid
erosion, bone grafting of the glenoid defect behind the baseplate or the use of
augmented baseplate components may allow for neutral or inferior tilt of the
glenosphere. However, other studies have not demonstrated improved results with
inferior tilt compared with neutral position if the component was placed in an inferior
position on the glenoid34 (Figure 13).

Cemented and ingrowth options are available for humeral fixation.
Cement fixation is commonly used in patients with osteoporosis.
The advantages of press-fit humeral stems with osteointegration include decreased surgical
time, biologic prosthetic fixation, and the avoidance of complications related to the use of
cement.

baseplate fixation, various options are available for humeral fixation. Cemented and

fixation. Cement fixation provides immediate stability and is commonly used in patients
with osteoporosis. Press-fit humeral stems with osteointegration have become more
common. The advantages of press-fit stems include decreased surgical time, biologic
prosthetic fixation, and avoidance of complications related to cement use.3 Given the
concern for maintaining humeral bone stock during revision procedures, shorter stem
humeral components recently have been introduced. Stemless humeral fixation also has
been used in Europe.36
Although humeral component loosening is not a common complication in patients who
undergo reverse shoulder arthroplasty, the rate of humeral component loosening after
reverse shoulder arthroplasty is twice as high that after anatomic shoulder
arthroplasty.3 This is believed to be the result of increased stress on the bone-implant
interface in the semiconstrained reverse shoulder arthroplasty design compared with an
anatomic design.37 In evaluating painful reverse shoulder arthroplasty implants with a
cemented stem, the cement-bone interface and the implant-cement interface should be
evaluated for signs of loosening.
Subscapularis Management
Repair of the subscapularis in patients undergoing reverse total shoulder arthroplasty is a
subject of controversy.
Repairing the subscapularis muscle counteracts the posterior rotator cuff muscles. Although
this may result in increased stability, concern exists that in the setting of weak external
rotators, subscapularis repair may lead to decreased active external rotation.
Many surgeons believe that the subscapularis should be repaired, if feasible, and not
excessively tensioned. In patients in whom this is not possible, consideration should be given
to prosthesis design to improve outcomes.

Repair of the subscapularis in patients undergoing reverse total shoulder arthroplasty
remains controversial. Theoretic advantages of repair include improving component
stability and internal rotation. Disadvantages of repair include decreasing external
rotation function and opposing deltoid function. Rotator cuff function may result in
increased stability of the joint and prosthesis;38,39 however, with distalization of the
humerus, the subscapularis force vector is placed below the center of the rotation,
causing it to act as a shoulder adductor. This opposes the role of the deltoid, resulting in
increased force required for forward elevation and abduction of the arm.
Similar to opposing deltoid function, repairing the anterior subscapularis also
counteracts the posterior rotator cuff muscles. This may lead to poor external rotation in
patients with poorly functioning posterior rotator cuff muscles.
The decision to repair the subscapularis is based on surgeon preference. Many surgeons
believe that the subscapularis should be repaired, if feasible, and not excessively
tensioned. In patients in whom this is not possible, consideration should be given to
prosthesis design to reduce instability and improve function.2

Increasing compressive forces of the components, depth of the humeral socket, and
glenosphere size affect the stability of the prosthesis.
Medial erosion of the glenoid may lead to decreased deltoid wrapping and decreased
compressive force of the deltoid and the intact rotator cuff.
Stability of the components is affected by patient and implant factors.

and implant factors.15,40 Early Grammont-style prostheses were associated with
dislocation rates as high as 30%.3 Lateralization of the humerus via the humeral
component or the glenosphere and baseplate may lead to increased compressive forces

Increasing the socket depth also may lead to impingement during range of motion.
Restoring Shoulder Rotation
Restoring external rotation of the shoulder is important for many activities of daily living.
Lateralized component design is intended to improve the length-tension relationship of the
infraspinatus and teres minor if they remain intact.
Muscle transfers are considered in posterior rotator cuff–deficient shoulders. The latissimus
dorsi is the muscle most transferred during reverse shoulder arthroplasty.

Restoring Shoulder Rotation
Restoring external rotation of the shoulder, in adduction and abduction, is an important
goal of reverse shoulder arthroplasty. This motion is important for many activities of
daily living, including eating and hygiene. Although the shoulder has four internal
rotators (subscapularis, teres major, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi), the shoulder
only has two external rotators (infraspinatus and teres minor). A lateralized component
design is intended to improve the length-tension relationship of the posterior rotator
cuff (infraspinatus and teres minor) if these muscles remain intact. In shoulders in which
these muscles are torn or otherwise deficient because of fatty degeneration, the deltoid
alone is insufficient to restore active external rotation, even with lateralized implants2
(Figure 14).

considered. The latissimus dorsi is the most commonly transferred muscle during
reverse shoulder arthroplasty. It is detached anteriorly from the humeral shaft, directed
posteriorly on the humerus, and reattached to the posterior proximal shaft or the
greater tuberosity. The L’Episcopo method, which involves transferring the latissimus
dorsi and the teres major to the greater tuberosity, also is occasionally used.

deficient shoulders.44,45 Increasing the retroversion of the humeral component will
increase the amount of external rotation and decrease the amount of internal rotation,
